nodes.label: Zagros metal ores
nodes.full: The Zagros mountains held silver, lead and copper ore deposits Mesopotamia's alluvial plain entirely lacked, giving Elam's economy a metal-producing base that Sumerian and Akkadian cities depended on importing — a structural economic advantage underlying Elam's persistent political relevance across the whole Bronze Age.
nodes.src: Zagros mining archaeology; comparative Mesopotamian textual evidence for imported metal dependency.

nodes.label: Tin and lapis transit
nodes.full: Elam's highland territory straddled the overland routes bringing tin from Central Asia and lapis lazuli from Badakhshan toward Mesopotamia, both essential to Bronze Age craft and prestige economies — control of this transit trade gave Elam consistent economic leverage over its lowland Mesopotamian neighbours regardless of who held the military advantage in any given decade.
nodes.src: Comparative sourcing studies of Bronze Age tin and lapis lazuli trade routes through the Iranian plateau.

nodes.label: Awan dynasty
nodes.full: Known chiefly from the Sumerian King List and a treaty with Naram-Sin of Akkad, the Awan kings ruled a Susa-centred Elamite state contemporary with Sargon's Akkadian empire — one of the earliest Elamite dynasties documented well enough to be dated and sequenced, even where most individual kings remain little more than names.
nodes.src: Sumerian King List, Awan dynasty section; the Naram-Sin–Elam treaty tablet, Louvre.

nodes.label: Naram-Sin treaty
nodes.full: The treaty between Naram-Sin of Akkad and an Elamite king, sworn by both the Mesopotamian and Elamite pantheons, formally ended a period of conflict between the two powers and bound the Elamite ruler as a subordinate ally — the occasion for the oldest surviving connected text written in the Elamite language.
nodes.src: Naram-Sin–Elam treaty tablet, Louvre Sb 8833.

nodes.label: Oldest Elamite text
nodes.full: The Naram-Sin–Elam treaty is the oldest known connected text written in the Elamite language, recorded in Akkadian cuneiform script — a linguistic milestone that lets historians confirm Elamite as a genuine, grammatically distinct language centuries before any Elamite-script text of comparable length survives.
nodes.src: Naram-Sin–Elam treaty tablet, Louvre Sb 8833; François Vallat, on the treaty's Elamite-language sections.

nodes.label: Bronze metallurgy
nodes.full: Direct access to Zagros copper and the tin trade routes passing through Elamite territory let Susa's smiths produce bronze tools and weapons at a scale and consistency that gave Elamite armies and craft production a real material advantage over metal-poor rivals further down the Mesopotamian plain.
nodes.src: Metallurgical analysis of Susa bronze artefact assemblages.

nodes.label: Puzur-Inshushinak
nodes.full: The last and most powerful Awan king, Puzur-Inshushinak briefly conquered large parts of southern Mesopotamia during Akkad's collapse, leaving royal inscriptions in both Akkadian and the newly invented Linear Elamite script — before Ur-Nammu of the rising Third Dynasty of Ur reversed his conquests entirely.
nodes.src: Puzur-Inshushinak royal inscriptions, Louvre and National Museum of Iran.

nodes.label: Mesopotamian campaigns
nodes.full: Exploiting the Akkadian Empire's collapse, Puzur-Inshushinak's inscriptions claim conquests reaching well into southern Mesopotamia — a high-water mark of Elamite military reach that proved as short-lived as the Akkadian power vacuum that had made it possible.
nodes.src: Puzur-Inshushinak royal inscriptions, on his claimed conquests.

nodes.label: Bilingual stelae
nodes.full: Puzur-Inshushinak commissioned stone stelae and statues carrying parallel Akkadian and Linear Elamite inscriptions — the two scripts placed side by side as a deliberate statement of a king who ruled, and wished to be read, in both the Mesopotamian and Elamite worlds at once.
nodes.src: Puzur-Inshushinak stelae, Louvre Sb 17 and related pieces.

nodes.label: Linear Elamite
nodes.full: Puzur-Inshushinak's inscriptions use Linear Elamite, a script distinct from both the earlier undeciphered proto-Elamite and Mesopotamian cuneiform, in use for barely a generation or two before falling out of use entirely — a 2022 collaborative decipherment finally made the script's roughly twenty signs and underlying Elamite readable after a century of failed attempts.
nodes.src: François Desset et al., 'The Decipherment of Linear Elamite Writing,' Zeitschrift für Assyriologie (2022).

nodes.label: Inshushinak
nodes.full: Puzur-Inshushinak's own name — 'servant of Inshushinak' — reflects the central place of Susa's patron deity in Elamite royal ideology from this early period onward; Inshushinak would remain the presiding god of Susa and a figure in Elamite royal titulature for the next fifteen centuries.
nodes.src: Puzur-Inshushinak royal inscriptions, invoking Inshushinak.

nodes.label: Akkadian-Elamite tablets
nodes.full: Susa's administrative and legal tablets from this period were written in both Akkadian and Elamite, sometimes within the same archive, reflecting a genuinely bilingual bureaucratic culture at the crossroads of the Elamite highlands and the Mesopotamian lowland tradition Susa had long been in contact with.
nodes.src: Susa administrative and legal tablet corpus, Louvre and National Museum of Iran.

nodes.label: Sukkalmah seals
nodes.full: Cylinder seals from Sukkalmah-period Susa show a distinctive local glyptic style — presentation scenes and geometric motifs adapted from, but visibly distinct from, contemporary Old Babylonian seal-cutting conventions — evidence of Elamite artisans absorbing Mesopotamian technique while maintaining a recognisably separate visual tradition.
nodes.src: Susa cylinder seal corpus, Louvre Museum; Pierre Amiet, Glyptique susienne (1972).

nodes.label: Shimashki dynasty
nodes.full: Succeeding Awan, the Shimashki kings are known largely through their culminating achievement: Kindattu's army sacked Ur in 2004 BC, capturing King Ibbi-Sin and ending the Third Dynasty of Ur — the single most consequential Elamite military success against Mesopotamia in the entire Bronze Age.
nodes.src: The Lament for Ur (Sumerian literary text); Elamite king list traditions preserved in later Mesopotamian sources.

nodes.label: Marriage alliances with Ur
nodes.full: Ur III kings gave royal daughters in marriage to Elamite rulers as part of a diplomatic strategy to manage the relationship with their powerful eastern neighbour — a policy that ultimately failed to prevent Kindattu's sack of Ur but demonstrates how seriously Mesopotamian kings took Elam as a diplomatic, not merely military, problem.
nodes.src: Ur III royal correspondence and year-name evidence for Elamite marriage alliances.

nodes.label: Royal women as diplomats
nodes.full: Princesses married across the Elamite-Mesopotamian frontier functioned as living diplomatic instruments, their marriages recorded in royal correspondence and year-names precisely because the alliances they embodied mattered to the states involved — political agency exercised through kinship rather than through any office the women held in their own right.
nodes.src: Ur III royal correspondence and year-name evidence for Elamite marriage alliances.

nodes.label: Kindattu sacks Ur
nodes.full: An Elamite army under Kindattu, joined by forces from Shimashki's allies, stormed Ur and carried King Ibbi-Sin into captivity in Elam — an event Sumerian scribes mourned for generations afterward in the 'Lament for the Destruction of Sumer and Ur,' ending the Third Dynasty of Ur and one of Mesopotamia's great imperial revivals.
nodes.src: The Lament for Ur; Sumerian King List, on the end of the Ur III dynasty.

nodes.label: Elam among the powers
nodes.full: Across this entire period Elam stood alongside Akkad, Ur and the Old Babylonian kingdom as one of the handful of states capable of shaping Near Eastern politics at the largest scale — sacking Ur outright, fielding coalition armies, and controlling trade routes no Mesopotamian power could bypass.
nodes.src: Comparative Bronze Age political history, Elam and its Mesopotamian contemporaries.

nodes.label: Susa-Anshan corridor
nodes.full: The route connecting lowland Susa to the highland city of Anshan in Fars, and onward toward Central Asia, functioned as Elam's own internal backbone as much as an external trade route — the two-centre geography of lowland Susa and highland Anshan would remain a defining structural feature of Elamite political organisation for its entire history.
nodes.src: Comparative settlement and trade-route studies linking Susa and Anshan (Tal-e Malyan).

nodes.label: Sukkalmah shared kingship
nodes.full: The long Sukkalmah (or Epartid) period governed Elam through a distinctive triarchic system — a sukkalmah ('grand regent') at Susa, a sukkal of Elam and Shimashki, and a sukkal of Susa itself, typically an uncle, nephew and brother — an institutionalised power-sharing arrangement with no real parallel in contemporary Mesopotamian kingship.
nodes.src: Sukkalmah-period administrative and legal tablets from Susa; Walther Hinz, 'The Elamite Sukkalmah Period,' Cambridge Ancient History.

nodes.label: Triarchic succession
nodes.full: Sukkalmah-period succession passed kingship laterally — typically from brother to brother before descending to the next generation's eldest nephew — rather than directly from father to son, a deliberate system that kept power within a wide circle of the royal family and may have reduced (without eliminating) succession disputes common under strict primogeniture.
nodes.src: Walther Hinz, 'The Elamite Sukkalmah Period,' Cambridge Ancient History, on the succession pattern reconstructed from dated tablets.

nodes.label: Royal temple dedications
nodes.full: Sukkalmah-era rulers recorded temple construction and dedication in their own royal inscriptions, continuing a pattern of kings legitimating their rule partly through visible religious patronage — the same basic logic of temple-building kingship attested across contemporary Mesopotamia, expressed in Elam's own religious idiom.
nodes.src: Sukkalmah-period royal building inscriptions, Susa.

nodes.label: Fortification of Susa
nodes.full: Sukkalmah-period Susa was enclosed within substantial defensive walls, reflecting a capital that needed to withstand both Mesopotamian counter-attacks and challenges from rival Elamite power centres on the plateau, such as Anshan, during a period when the dynasty's authority was real but not absolute.
nodes.src: Susa excavation reports, on Sukkalmah-period fortification remains.

nodes.label: Corvee labour at Susa
nodes.full: Sukkalmah-period Susa's fortifications and temple construction, like comparable Mesopotamian building projects of the era, almost certainly depended on conscripted corvée labour drawn from the general population — a form of compulsory service the surviving administrative tablets record in terms of labour-quotas rather than individual experience.
nodes.src: Comparative Bronze Age Near Eastern corvée labour practice, inferred from Susa's administrative tablet corpus.

nodes.label: Hammurabi beats coalition
nodes.full: Hammurabi's own year-names record a decisive victory over an alliance including Elam, Assyria and other regional powers — a reversal of the earlier alliance in which an Elamite-backed coalition had helped Hammurabi's Babylon against Larsa, showing how quickly the era's shifting alignments could turn former allies into declared enemies.
nodes.src: Hammurabi's year-name list, on the defeat of the Elamite coalition.

nodes.label: End of Sukkalmah order
nodes.full: The Sukkalmah system's triarchic power-sharing gradually gave way around 1500 BC to more conventional father-to-son kingship under the rulers who would found the Middle Elamite kingdom — a transition in the mechanics of succession as significant, in its own way, as any single battle in this folio.
nodes.src: Elamite king-list reconstructions, on the Sukkalmah-to-Middle-Elamite transition.

nodes.label: Akkadian Empire collapses
nodes.full: The fall of the Akkadian Empire left a power vacuum across southern Mesopotamia that Elamite kings exploited.
nodes.src: background — see the Mesopotamia 2334–2004 BC folio

nodes.label: Ur III rises
nodes.full: Ur-Nammu’s Third Dynasty of Ur reverses Elamite conquests and later manages Elam through royal marriage diplomacy.
nodes.src: named in this folio’s p2 and x1; see the Mesopotamia 2334–2004 BC folio
